record.evidence_description: Git's own normative definitions of the object database and its four object types. States that an object is identified by its object name, that a blob is an untyped object, that a tree lists names and modes with refs to blobs and trees, that a commit contains parents and a tree, that commit objects form a DAG, that the index is a collection of files with stat information whose contents are stored as objects, and that reachability follows tags to their targets, commits to parents and trees, and trees to their contents.
record.label: git gitglossary(7), git 2.50.1
record.locator: entries: blob object; commit object; DAG; dangling object; index; index entry; object database; object identifier; object name; object type; reachable; tree object

record.evidence_description: Normative pack format. States that conceptually there are only four object types and that an object may be stored as a delta of a base object to save space; distinguishes OBJ_OFS_DELTA from OBJ_REF_DELTA; states that a base object may itself be deltified within the same pack, that ref-delta may point outside the pack in a thin pack, and that an on-disk pack should be self contained.
record.label: git gitformat-pack(5), git 2.50.1
record.locator: sections: CHECKSUMS AND OBJECT IDS; PACK-*.PACK FILES HAVE THE FOLLOWING FORMAT; Object types; Deltified representation; Original (version 1) pack-*.idx files; Version 2 pack-*.idx files

record.evidence_description: On-disk layout. States that an object store is usually self sufficient, that loose objects are splayed over 256 directories by the first two characters of the object name, that packs store many objects in compressed form with index files allowing random access, and that git prune preserves objects reachable from refs.
record.label: git gitrepository-layout(5), git 2.50.1
record.locator: entries: objects; objects/[0-9a-f][0-9a-f]; objects/pack; objects/info/alternates; refs; index

record.evidence_description: Git's own plumbing tutorial. States 'Objects are immutable.' and, introducing git repack, states 'Since Git objects are immutable once they are created, there is a way to optimize the storage by "packing them together"'. This makes packing an explicitly post-hoc storage optimization over an already-immutable object set.
record.label: git gitcore-tutorial(7), git 2.50.1

record.evidence_description: Reclamation policy. Housekeeping removes unreachable objects; loose objects are pruned only after a default two-week grace period (gc.pruneExpire, prune --expire 2.weeks.ago); unreachable objects are by default written to a separate cruft pack rather than deleted immediately, and the grace period exists to prevent corruption when gc runs concurrently with a writer.
record.label: git git-gc(1), git 2.50.1

record.evidence_description: Reproducible probe with fixed author identity and fixed commit dates. A: hash preimage. B: two unrelated repositories reaching identical content. C: two branches reconverging on identical content. D: 31 revisions of one file, loose then packed, with delta chains and full-text bases mapped to their revision numbers. E: reachability, reflog and prune. F: index deletion and reconstruction. G: object-set signature under three pack encodings. H: full-text base after a forced repack.
record.label: Local git object-database probe, script
notes: Written for this review, not a third-party artifact. Run against git version 2.50.1 (Apple Git-155) on macOS 24.6.0.

record.evidence_description: Captured output of the probe. Two consecutive runs of this script produced byte-identical output apart from the temporary working directory path.
record.label: Local git object-database probe, recorded output

record.evidence_description: An earlier run of the same probe up to section F. Every object name matches the later run, but the pack produced by git gc placed a different revision at depth 0 as the full-text delta base (acc590a5..., 194446 bytes) than the later runs did (458f9358..., 194471 bytes). Retained as the evidence that pack delta assignment varied across runs while object names did not.
record.label: Local git object-database probe, earlier run without sections G and H
notes: The two runs differ only in reporting code added after the pack was built. This review did not isolate the cause of the differing delta assignment and does not claim git's packing is nondeterministic in general.

record.axis_definition: The function that produces a node's identifier. Content of the state it denotes; the operation or answer that produced it; a sequence number or position; or an externally minted opaque id. Question: given only a node's identity, what can be concluded about it without reading the store?
record.label: What names a stored node

record.axis_definition: Whether two independently produced but equal artifacts become one stored artifact with no coordination, comparison pass, or merge step, and at which layer that happens. Question: does equality of content force equality of identity?
record.label: Automatic convergence of equal things

record.axis_definition: Whether a version is modelled as a complete state or as a change relative to another version, and whether that choice is semantic (the model's unit of meaning) or an encoding detail invisible above the storage layer.
record.label: Snapshot or change as the primary unit

record.axis_definition: The structure history takes: a DAG of immutable nodes each naming its predecessors; a linear append-only log; a per-item revision list; or an unordered or partially-ordered set of operations. Question: what does 'this happened after that' mean structurally?
record.label: Shape of recorded history

record.axis_definition: Whether a subset of recorded steps can be extracted, reordered, or replayed onto a different base as a first-class operation with defined semantics, versus being a derived operation that reconstructs new nodes and may fail or conflict.
record.label: Selecting, reordering and reapplying recorded steps

record.axis_definition: What must be recomputed, replayed, or reconstructed to obtain a usable state at an arbitrary recorded point, and what the store does about that cost (materialized states, periodic snapshots, delta chain depth caps, or nothing).
record.label: Cost of obtaining a usable state at a point

record.axis_definition: Whether the identifier of a node cryptographically certifies its contents and, transitively, everything it references, so that verification is a byproduct of lookup rather than a separate mechanism.
record.label: Integrity carried by the naming scheme

record.axis_definition: Whether the system distinguishes an authoritative store from derived indexes and caches, and whether every derived structure can be discarded and rebuilt from the authority alone.
record.label: Separation of authority from index

record.axis_definition: How the store decides what may be deleted: reachability from a set of named roots, a retention or expiry policy, explicit deletion, or never. Question: what makes a recorded node worth keeping?
record.label: Rule for deleting recorded material
Decision-tape store: append-only per-run answer logs with shared prefixes and recorded legal alternatives
notes: The target is the reviewer's declared design problem, not a published work. Its axis profile records what the tape store already commits to, so the set comparison against each candidate model is exact rather than rhetorical.
record.review_method: Primary-source inspection of git's own shipped documentation on the local installation (git 2.50.1, man page files digested by sha256), plus a written, reproducible probe against a live git binary whose script and output are stored in this project, plus web inspection of origin correspondence, format documentation, and the primary literature for the alternative models. Coverage levels are coded per axis for each work and for the target itself.
record.scope: A tape is an append-only JSONL file: one line per decision taken during a run, plus a seed. Every other property of the run is derived from the seed and the recorded answers, so replaying the answers reproduces the run exactly. Each entry also records which other answers were legal at that moment. Many runs share long identical prefixes and diverge at a single decision. The design question under review is what storage model the tape store should be built on. Compare git's object model, its acknowledged and probable ancestors, and the two genuinely different models available (a history of patches, and an event log with derived read models) against nine axes covering identity, convergence, unit of storage, history shape, selective replay, derivation cost, integrity, authority, and reclamation. This review does not decide the design; it records what each model commits to and what the evidence shows.

record.label: Git object database (blobs, trees, commits, tags; refs; packfiles; index)
record.priority_date_basis: Date of git's first commit, e83c5163316f89bfbde7d9ab23ca2e25604af290, 'Initial revision of git, the information manager from hell'. Recorded here as the first-public date of the object model; the local artifact inspected is version 2.50.1.
record.title: Git object database as documented and as observed at version 2.50.1

record.label: An object's name is a hash over a type-and-length header plus the exact bytes, and nothing else
record.statement: A git object's name is SHA-1 (or SHA-256 in a SHA-256 repository) over the byte string '<type> <byte-length>\0<content>'. No filename, path, timestamp, author, or history enters the name. The probe reproduced the object name of a six-byte file by hashing 'blob 6\0hello\n' outside git and got the identical 40-hex name, and inflating the loose object file yielded exactly that preimage.

record.label: The object database has exactly four types
record.statement: Blob, tree, commit and tag are the only object types. gitformat-pack states 'Conceptually there are only four object types: commit, tree, tag and blob'; the two additional pack type codes, OBJ_OFS_DELTA and OBJ_REF_DELTA, are storage representations valid only inside a pack file and are not object types in the database sense.

record.label: A blob is untyped bytes; the name and mode live in the referring tree
record.statement: gitglossary defines a blob object as an 'Untyped object, e.g. the contents of a file' and a tree object as 'An object containing a list of file names and modes along with refs to the associated blob and/or tree objects'. The probe confirmed that copying a file to a second filename yields the same blob name, so identity is content, and structure is one level up.

record.label: A commit's name covers state, lineage, and metadata together
record.statement: A commit object contains one tree name, zero or more parent commit names, author and committer identities with timestamps, and a message. Because the object name is a hash of that whole body, the commit name is a function of the state, the entire ancestry, and the metadata simultaneously. The probe printed two commit bodies showing 'tree <oid>' and 'parent <oid>' lines verbatim.

record.label: Git converges state automatically and refuses to converge history
notes: This is the load-bearing observation for the review target. Git does not answer 'key by the answer or by the resulting state' with one choice; it keys the state layer by state and the history layer by answer-plus-ancestry, and lets the first deduplicate underneath the second.
record.statement: Git splits identity across two layers. Blobs and trees name state, so equal states collapse to one stored object with no coordination. Commits name state plus ancestry plus metadata, so equal states reached by different routes stay distinct forever. The probe demonstrated both halves: two repositories that never communicated produced the same tree name 68ba7e4f... by different commit routes and different commit names; and inside one repository, two branches that arrived at byte-identical content produced the same tree 72334f9a... under two different commit names.

record.label: Deduplication needs no comparison pass and no shared registry
record.statement: Because the name is a pure function of content, two stores that never communicated assign the same name to the same bytes. The probe built two repositories independently and found identical blob names (4a580070..., 65b2df87...) and an identical tree name for the resulting directory. Sharing is therefore a property of the naming scheme, not of a merge, an interning table, or a background dedup job.

record.label: Objects are immutable once written
record.statement: gitcore-tutorial states plainly: 'Objects are immutable.' and, when introducing repacking, 'Since Git objects are immutable once they are created, there is a way to optimize the storage by "packing them together"'. Writing is therefore add-only; nothing already named is ever edited in place.

record.label: The packfile is an encoding of an object set, not part of any object's identity
record.statement: The probe computed a signature over every object name, type and size in a repository under three different pack encodings: the default gc pack with deltas, a forcibly delta-free repack, and a normal repack. All three produced the identical signature d519f453... while the on-disk size moved between 44 KB and 340 KB. The pack format is therefore a compression and locality decision that commits to nothing semantically.

record.label: Delta bases are chosen by the packer, not by history position
notes: An earlier run of the same probe produced a different full-text base for the same object set. This review did not isolate why and does not claim that git's delta selection is nondeterministic in general; the recorded point is only that the choice is the packer's and is not derivable from the commit graph.
record.statement: In the probe's 31-revision repository, git gc stored two blobs whole (revision 1 and revision 18 of 31) and expressed the other 29 as deltas in chains up to depth 7, with several revisions deltifying against a base many revisions away. gitformat-pack confirms the freedom: a base may itself be deltified inside the same pack, and a ref-delta in a thin pack may even name a base outside the pack. Delta structure and history structure are independent.

record.label: Deltas, not zlib, carry the bulk of the space saving for near-identical versions
record.statement: Thirty-one revisions of one ~190 KB file occupied 620 KiB as loose zlib-compressed objects and 30.4 KiB after git gc. Repacking the identical object set with deltas disabled produced 340 KiB. So zlib alone gave roughly 1.8x and delta compression gave a further 7.7x. Storing many near-identical states costs approximately the size of their differences, but only after the packer runs.

record.label: All mutation is confined to refs
record.statement: The object graph never changes; branches are mutable named pointers into it, stored under refs. gitrepository-layout states that git prune preserves objects reachable from refs found in the refs directory, and gitglossary defines a branch's tip as referenced by a branch head that moves forward as development proceeds. Advancing a branch is a pointer write, not a rewrite of history.

record.label: Liveness is reachability from named roots, with a grace period
record.statement: gitglossary defines reachability as following tags to their targets, commits to their parents and trees, and trees to their contents. git-gc removes unreachable objects but only after a default two-week grace period (gc.pruneExpire, prune --expire 2.weeks.ago) and by default writes them to a separate cruft pack rather than deleting them at once. The probe deleted a branch, found its tip still readable while the reflog referenced it, and found it gone only after expiring the reflog and running gc --prune=now.

record.label: The index is a rebuildable cache, except while a merge is unresolved
record.statement: gitglossary calls the index 'A collection of files with stat information, whose contents are stored as objects', i.e. it holds object names plus stat data, not content. The probe deleted .git/index entirely, rebuilt it with git read-tree from the commit, and got the identical tree name back. The exception is stated in the same entry: the index 'can also contain a second, and even a third version of a working tree, which are used when merging', so during an unresolved merge it holds state that exists in no tree.

record.label: There is no per-path revision structure; file history is derived by walking and diffing
notes: Coded as reviewer inference from the object type definitions and the on-disk layout, both of which describe an object store with no path-indexed structure. The reviewer did not audit every optional auxiliary index git can build (commit-graph, multi-pack-index, reachability bitmaps) for a path-indexed variant; those are named in the inspected pages as ancillary indexes.
record.statement: None of the four object types records a per-path revision list: a blob is contentless of its own name, a tree is one directory at one instant, a commit points at one whole tree, and a tag points at one object. The history of a path is therefore not stored; it is computed by walking commits and comparing trees. This is the direct structural consequence of choosing whole-state snapshots as the unit.

record.label: One name fixes every byte reachable from it
record.statement: Because each object's name hashes its bytes, and its bytes include the names of the objects it references, a commit name is a hash over its tree name, which is a hash over its entries' names, and so on. Naming a commit therefore fixes the whole reachable subgraph: no content anywhere under it can change without changing the name. Verification is a byproduct of lookup rather than an added mechanism.

record.basis: gitglossary defines the object name as the unique identifier of an object; the probe reproduced the preimage byte-for-byte outside git.
Stated verbatim in gitformat-pack's Deltified representation section and in gitglossary's object type entry.
gitglossary states the blob is untyped and the tree carries names and modes; the probe showed a copied file keeps the same blob name.
gitglossary's commit object entry names parents, committer, author, date and tree as the contents; the probe printed the raw commit bodies.

Git's documentation states the parts (content-named objects; commits containing parents) but does not state the two-layer consequence as such. The consequence was established directly by the probe, which exhibited a shared tree name under two distinct commit names in two separate constructions.
Established by construction in the probe: two repositories built independently produced identical blob and tree names.
gitcore-tutorial states 'Objects are immutable.' in the plumbing walkthrough.

gitcore-tutorial frames packing as an optimization enabled by immutability; the probe established invariance of the object-set signature across three encodings, which the documentation does not state as such.
gitformat-pack states the structural freedom (chained bases, thin packs); the probe measured which revisions actually became full-text bases in a concrete pack.
Measured in the probe on one synthetic corpus of 31 revisions of one file; the ratio is specific to that corpus and is recorded as such.
gitrepository-layout and gitglossary describe refs as the moving pointers and the roots prune preserves.
Definition in gitglossary, policy in git-gc, behaviour confirmed in the probe.
Both halves are in gitglossary's index entry; the reconstruction was verified in the probe.
Inferred from the four object type definitions and the on-disk layout, neither of which contains a path-indexed revision structure. Not stated as an absence by the inspected pages.
Follows from the hash preimage established in the probe plus the reference structure defined in gitglossary; the inspected git pages describe the structure without naming the property.
Every object is named by a hash of its own bytes with a type-and-length header, verified byte-for-byte in the probe. Identity is content, exclusively.

Equal states collapse with zero coordination at the blob and tree layer, demonstrated across two unrelated repositories and across two branches in one repository; equal states never collapse at the commit layer.

The semantic unit is a whole-tree snapshot: a commit names one complete tree. Deltas exist only inside packs, are chosen by the packer, and change no object's name. Git answers this axis by putting snapshots in the model and deltas in the encoding.

gitglossary: commit objects form a directed acyclic graph because they have parents and no chain begins and ends with the same object. Each node names its predecessors inside the bytes that determine its own name.

The object model contains no movable change object. A commit is welded to its parents by its own name, so cherry-pick and rebase cannot move a commit; they compute a diff, apply it elsewhere, and mint new commits with new names. Selective replay exists as porcelain behaviour, not as a modelled operation, which is why this axis is coded PARTIAL rather than CENTRAL.

Reading a state at an arbitrary point requires no replay: the commit names a tree that already denotes the full state. Cost reappears only inside the pack, bounded by delta chain depth (depth 7 in the probe's pack), and is invisible above the object layer.
Names hash bytes, and bytes contain the names of referenced objects, so a commit name transitively fixes its entire reachable subgraph. Verification is a byproduct of lookup.

The object store is the authority; the staging index, pack index files, commit-graph and multi-pack-index are derived and rebuildable. The probe deleted the index and reconstructed it from a commit to the same tree name. The one documented exception is an unresolved merge, whose second and third index stages exist in no tree.

Reachability from refs decides liveness; unreachable objects survive a two-week default grace period and are moved to a cruft pack rather than deleted at once. Nothing is deleted because it was superseded, only because nothing names it any more.

Stated as the first open question of the design: is a node keyed by the answer taken, or by the resulting state? Today a tape line records an answer and the legal alternatives at that moment; nothing in the tape is keyed by the world it produces.
notes: Evidence is attached only to satisfy the relation's evidence requirement; the target's profile comes from the reviewer's declared design brief, not from an inspected artifact. Reading the tape implementation itself was out of scope for this pass by instruction.

record.basis: Stated in the brief: two different answers can converge on the same resulting world, and the question is whether the store should notice. Convergence is therefore a live requirement, not an incidental property.
The tape already commits to the change side of this axis: one line is one decision, and no line contains a world. The world is a derived quantity, recovered by replaying answers against the seed.

Stated in the brief: many runs share long identical prefixes and diverge at one decision. That is a prefix tree over answer sequences, which becomes a DAG only if converging states are merged, which is exactly the first open question.

Recording the legal alternatives at each decision means the store is expected to support 'replay this prefix, then take a different branch'. Whether it must also support extracting or reordering decisions out of sequence is not stated in the brief and was not established here.

Stated in the brief: the resulting world is expensive to compute. Since the tape stores only answers, obtaining the world at a point requires replaying the prefix through the engine. Derivation cost is therefore central, and it is the axis on which the tape differs most sharply from git.

The brief states no requirement for tamper evidence, signing, untrusted transport, or third-party verification of a tape. NOT_ESTABLISHED records that this review did not establish the requirement; it is not a finding that integrity is unwanted. This matters because integrity is the single property git's naming scheme buys most decisively, and if it is not required, the strongest argument for hashing is not in play.

Stated as the second open question: is the store a file format, or is it derived on demand from a directory of tapes? The tapes themselves are already an authority; what is undecided is whether anything durable sits beside them.

The brief says nothing about deleting tapes or reclaiming space, and an append-only JSONL directory has no reachability notion of its own. Recorded as NOT_ESTABLISHED rather than as an absence of need.

record.evidence_description: The message announcing that the kernel would leave BitKeeper. States that the BitKeeper conflict had not worked out and that the kernel team is looking at alternatives, asks readers not to blame BitMover, and closes with the postscript: 'Don't bother telling me about subversion. If you must, start reading up on "monotone". That seems to be the most viable alternative'. Dated one day before git's first commit.
record.label: Linus Torvalds, 'Kernel SCM saga..', LKML, 2005-04-06
record.locator: LKML thread 'Kernel SCM saga..', message of 2005-04-06 15:42:08 UTC, opening paragraphs and postscript
notes: lore.kernel.org is behind a proof-of-work challenge and was not fetchable in this pass; marc.info was used as the archive mirror.

record.evidence_description: Contemporary third-party account, dated 2005-04-06, that BitMover decided it could no longer make BitKeeper available to the free software community, which is the event that put the kernel in need of a new tool.
record.label: LWN, 'The kernel and BitKeeper part ways', 2005-04-06
notes: Read through a page-summarising fetch rather than extracted from raw bytes. The date and the substance are recorded; exact wording is not byte-verified and is not quoted as verbatim anywhere in this project.

record.evidence_description: Design message written two days into the work. On monotone: 'it doesn't actually seem to be _doing_ anything while it's slow ... It seems to have some exponential function on the number of pathnames involved', and 'I'm hoping they can fix it, though. The basic notions do not sound wrong.' On what he was building: 'Another way of looking at it is to say that it's really a content-addressable filesystem, used to track directory trees', 'Never mind merging. It's not an SCM, it's a distribution and archival mechanism', and 'The database is designed so that you can do the equivalent of a nonmerging (ie pure superset) push/pull with just plain rsync'.
record.label: Linus Torvalds, 'Re: Kernel SCM saga..', LKML, 2005-04-07
record.locator: LKML archive stamp Thu Apr 07 2005 - 23:41:58 EST

record.evidence_description: The rename decision, stated as a design choice rather than an omission: 'GIT doesn't care. There is _zero_ space efficiency in trying to track renames. In fact, it would add overhead to the system, not lessen it. That's because GIT fundamentally doesn't do the "delta-within-a-file" model.' Also 'So consider me deficient, or consider me radical. It boils down to the same thing. Renames don't matter.' and 'I really really designed it coming at the problem from the viewpoint of a _filesystem_ person'.
record.label: Linus Torvalds, 'Re: more git updates..', LKML, 2005-04-10
record.locator: LKML archive stamp Sun Apr 10 2005 - 10:44:22 EST, reply to Junio C Hamano
notes: The hypermail header stamp and the timestamp quoted in a reply differ by about an hour; the date 2005-04-10 is not in doubt.

record.evidence_description: The clearest primary statement of why history is kept out of content objects: 'There fundamentally is no history in objects, _except_ for the commit object. Two objects with the same name are identical, and that means that they are easy to share.' and 'Any time you break that model, you break the whole point of git ... because it breaks the clean separation of "time" and "space".'
record.label: Linus Torvalds, 'Re: Handling renames.', git list, 2005-04-14

record.evidence_description: States the naming principle and its consequence for what git models: 'It's fundamentally the git notion of "content determines objects"' and 'A "rename" really doesn't exist in the git model. The git model really is about tracking data, not about tracking what happened to _create_ that data.'
record.label: Linus Torvalds, 'Re: Handling renames.', git list, 2005-04-14 (earlier message)

record.evidence_description: The replacement mechanism for the rejected feature: 'let's just posit that "files" do not matter. The only thing that matters is how "content" moved in the tree', and 'that "where did this come from" decision should be done at _search_ time, not commit time.' Provenance is recomputed on demand from content rather than recorded at write time.
record.label: Linus Torvalds, 'Re: Merge with git-pasky II.', git list, 2005-04-15

record.evidence_description: The design document written with the code on 2005-04-07. States 'GIT - the stupid content tracker'; 'The object database is literally just a content-addressable collection of objects. All objects are named by their content, which is approximated by the SHA1 hash of the object itself'; 'The SHA1 hash is always the hash of the _compressed_ object, not the original one'; 'the tree object is uniquely determined by the set contents, and so two separate but identical trees will always share the exact same object'; 'The "changeset" object is an object that introduces the notion of history into the picture'; 'unlike real SCM's, changesets do not contain rename information or file mode chane information. All of that is implicit in the trees involved'; and, under TRUST, 'a single named changeset specifies uniquely a whole set of history, with full contents. You can't later fake any step of the way once you have the name of a changeset' and "'git' itself only handles content integrity, the trust has to come from outside".
record.label: git README at the first commit, e83c5163
record.locator: sections: title line; opening paragraph; 'The Object Database (SHA1_FILE_DIRECTORY)'; 'TREE:'; 'CHANGESET:'; 'Note on changesets:'; 'TRUST:'
notes: At this commit the object store lived under .dircache/ and the history object was called a 'changeset', not a 'commit'.

record.evidence_description: Direct code check of the 2005 hashing order. The function deflates the buffer first (deflateInit, deflate to Z_FINISH, deflateEnd, size = stream.total_out) and only then computes SHA1_Init, SHA1_Update(&c, compressed, size), SHA1_Final. The 2005 object name is therefore the hash of the compressed bytes, confirming the README's statement against the producer rather than against a description of it.
record.label: git read-cache.c at the first commit, e83c5163

record.evidence_description: The preserved design discussion of the packer's heuristics. Junio: 'and finally sort by size, larger to smaller' and 'we prefer to delta against larger objects, so that we have lots of removals'. Linus, separating placement from delta choice: 'The recency ordering (which is basically: put objects _physically_ into the pack in the order that they are "reachable" from the head) is important' but 'recency ordering is totally useless for deciding how to actually generate the deltas, so the delta ordering is something else.'
record.label: git Documentation/technical/pack-heuristics.adoc
record.locator: IRC transcript, Junio C Hamano and Linus Torvalds on delta selection and packing order

record.evidence_description: The widely read account of delta direction: 'When Git packs objects, it looks for files that are named and sized similarly, and stores just the deltas from one version of the file to the next', and, on a worked example, that the second (newer) version of the file is the one stored intact while the original is stored as a delta, 'because you're most likely to need faster access to the most recent version of the file'.
record.label: Pro Git 2nd edition, 10.4 Packfiles

record.evidence_description: Git's own statement of what content addressing buys and what it costs. Buys: 'Integrity checking is easy. Bit flips, for example, are easily detected, as the hash of corrupted content does not match its name' and 'Object names can be signed and third parties can trust the hash to address the signed object and all objects it references.' Costs: the SHAttered collision of 23 February 2017, the move to a hardened SHA-1 in v2.13.0, and the statement that if SHA-1 were truly broken 'we could not trust that a given hash value represented the known good version of content that the speaker intended'. SHA-256 was picked as the successor in late 2018. Stated requirements: collision and second-preimage resistance, not length-extension resistance.
record.label: git Documentation/technical/hash-function-transition.adoc

record.evidence_description: Dedup stated by git's own manual: 'Since the blob is entirely defined by its data, if two files in a directory tree (or in multiple different versions of the repository) have the same contents, they will share the same blob object. The object is totally independent of its location in the directory tree, and renaming a file does not change the object that file is associated with.' Trust: 'the immutability of the history of commits tells others that they can trust the whole history' and that a whole archive can be validated by publishing the name of the top commit and signing that.
record.label: git Documentation/user-manual.adoc, Blob Object and Trust sections

record.evidence_description: States that prune runs fsck --unreachable using the refs available and prunes unpacked objects unreachable from those heads, and adds: 'Note that unreachable, packed objects will remain. If this is not desired, see git-repack(1).' Reclamation therefore depends on where an object physically sits, not only on reachability.
record.label: git git-prune(1), git 2.50.1

record.label: Linus Torvalds' April 2005 design correspondence on LKML and the git list
notes: Public mailing-list correspondence, not a publication. Recorded as a Work because it is the primary record of the design decisions and their stated reasons.
record.priority_date_basis: Date of the earliest message in the set, 'Kernel SCM saga..' of 2005-04-06 15:42:08 UTC. The set runs to 2005-04-15.
record.title: April 2005 design correspondence: Kernel SCM saga, more git updates, Handling renames, Merge with git-pasky II

record.label: History is deliberately excluded from content objects so that equal content can be shared
record.statement: Linus Torvalds stated the reason for keeping history out of everything except the commit object: 'There fundamentally is no history in objects, _except_ for the commit object. Two objects with the same name are identical, and that means that they are easy to share.' He described any change to that as breaking 'the clean separation of "time" and "space"'. Sharing is not an emergent benefit of content addressing; it is the stated purpose of excluding history from the objects that carry content.

record.label: Convergence of identical trees was an explicit day-one property
record.statement: The first commit's README already states it: 'the tree object is uniquely determined by the set contents, and so two separate but identical trees will always share the exact same object.' Convergence of equal state was designed in at the start, not discovered later.

record.label: Rename tracking was rejected on purpose, and provenance moved to query time
record.statement: Git's most-criticised omission was a decision with a stated reason. 'There is _zero_ space efficiency in trying to track renames ... That's because GIT fundamentally doesn't do the "delta-within-a-file" model'; 'A "rename" really doesn't exist in the git model. The git model really is about tracking data, not about tracking what happened to _create_ that data'; and the replacement: 'that "where did this come from" decision should be done at _search_ time, not commit time.' Recording what happened was rejected in favour of recording what is, and recovering what happened by search.

record.label: Monotone was named as the alternative and rejected on speed; no primary statement of borrowing was found
notes: NOT ESTABLISHED is not proof of absence. A statement of borrowing may exist in sources this pass did not reach, including the 2007 Google Tech Talk and later interviews.
record.statement: The primary record establishes that Linus Torvalds pointed the list at monotone on 2005-04-06 ('start reading up on "monotone". That seems to be the most viable alternative'), and that a day later he rejected it on performance while accepting its ideas ('monotone really _is_ that slow'; 'The basic notions do not sound wrong'). This review did not find a primary statement by Torvalds that git's content-addressed object naming was taken from monotone. The frequently repeated claim that git borrowed content addressing from monotone is therefore NOT ESTABLISHED here; what is established is proximity, a pointer, and an explicit rejection on speed.

record.label: Git was first described as a content-addressable filesystem and a distribution mechanism, not an SCM
record.statement: Two days into the work Torvalds wrote: 'Another way of looking at it is to say that it's really a content-addressable filesystem, used to track directory trees' and 'Never mind merging. It's not an SCM, it's a distribution and archival mechanism.' Replication was a design target from the start: 'The database is designed so that you can do the equivalent of a nonmerging (ie pure superset) push/pull with just plain rsync.' A store whose objects are named by content and never mutate can be replicated by a dumb file copier.

record.label: Git originally hashed the compressed bytes; today it hashes the canonical uncompressed form
notes: The commit that made the change was not identified. A listing of git.git commits touching read-cache.c up to 2005-05-15 was inspected and contains no such subject line; the change may sit outside that window or in another file. Recorded as NOT ESTABLISHED, not as absence.
record.statement: At the first commit the object name was the SHA-1 of the deflated bytes: write_sha1_file() in read-cache.c deflates first and then calls SHA1_Update on the compressed buffer, and the README says so in words ('The SHA1 hash is always the hash of the _compressed_ object, not the original one'). At git 2.50.1 the name is the SHA-1 of the uncompressed preimage: the probe reproduced an object name by hashing 'blob 6\0hello\n' outside git. Hashing the encoding makes identity depend on the compressor's version and settings; hashing a canonical uncompressed form does not. Git moved from the first to the second.

record.label: Delta bases are picked by a size-ordered sort; recency governs physical placement only
record.statement: git's own pack-heuristics transcript separates the two orderings. Junio C Hamano on delta selection: 'and finally sort by size, larger to smaller' and 'we prefer to delta against larger objects, so that we have lots of removals'. Linus Torvalds on placement: recency ordering puts objects physically into the pack in reachability order from the head, but 'recency ordering is totally useless for deciding how to actually generate the deltas, so the delta ordering is something else.' Pro Git's account, that the newest version is stored intact for faster access, describes the common outcome (files usually grow, so newest is usually largest) rather than the selection rule. The probe's result is consistent with the size rule and not with a recency rule: the whole-stored bases were revisions 1 and 18 of 31, not revision 31.

record.label: Content addressing buys integrity and signing, and owes a hash migration
record.statement: git's hash-function-transition document names the payoff: 'Integrity checking is easy. Bit flips, for example, are easily detected, as the hash of corrupted content does not match its name', and 'Object names can be signed and third parties can trust the hash to address the signed object and all objects it references.' It also names the bill: SHAttered demonstrated a practical SHA-1 collision on 23 February 2017, git moved to a hardened SHA-1 in v2.13.0, SHA-256 was chosen as successor in late 2018, and the transition is still being carried. Putting a cryptographic function in the identity layer means every identifier ever published depends on that function's continued strength.

record.label: Naming gives content integrity; trust must come from outside
record.statement: The first README drew the line that git still holds: 'a single named changeset specifies uniquely a whole set of history, with full contents. You can't later fake any step of the way once you have the name of a changeset', but also "'git' itself only handles content integrity, the trust has to come from outside." The current user manual restates it: publish and sign the name of the top commit and the whole archive is validated.

record.label: Reachability decides liveness, but packing decides whether prune can act
record.statement: git-prune's own description states: 'Note that unreachable, packed objects will remain. If this is not desired, see git-repack(1).' Deletion is therefore not a pure function of reachability; it depends on whether the object is loose or already inside a pack, which is a storage-layer fact. Reclamation in git is reachability plus a grace period plus a physical-layout condition.

Same system, twenty-one years apart. The four object types, content naming, tree convergence and the trust argument survive verbatim from the first README into the shipped documentation. Two things changed: the hash preimage moved from the compressed bytes to the canonical uncompressed form, and 'changeset' became 'commit'.
The correspondence of 2005-04-06 to 2005-04-15 states the design decisions that the shipped object model implements.
